en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on the Buddha, concerning the Question of Inference.

5. The Question on Turning Back to the Lesser Vehicle “Venerable Nāgasena, this teaching of the Tathāgata is vast, essential, excellent, supreme, sublime, incomparable, pure, stainless, bright, and blameless.
It is not fitting that one who is a householder should be ordained for such a long time; it is only for householders [to remain so].”
Once he has been trained in one fruit, when he becomes one who does not return, then he may be ordained.
For what reason?
Because these wicked people, having gone forth into this pure Teaching, turn back and return to the lower life.
"Because they are returning, this great multitude thinks thus: 'Alas, sirs, this teaching of the ascetic Gotama must surely be empty, since these people are turning back. This is the reason here.
"Suppose, Great King, there were a lake filled with pure, stainless, cool water; then some person who was defiled..."
“Suppose, Great King, a man who had fallen into mud and mire went to that pond, and without bathing, returned covered in filth.
In this case, Great King, whom would people blame: the man who was filthy, or the pond?

“The people, venerable sir, would blame the filthy man, saying: ‘This man went to the pond and returned without bathing, still filthy. Why should the pond itself bathe him when he does not wish to bathe? What fault is there in the pond?’”
“In the same way, Great King, the Tathāgata constructed a noble pond of the True Dhamma, filled with the excellent water of liberation, thinking:
‘Whatever sentient beings are wise and defiled by the stains of the defilements, having bathed here, they will wash away all their defilements.
If anyone, having gone to that noble pond of the True Dhamma, were to turn back and return to the lower life still defiled, without having bathed—”
People will indeed censure him, saying: "Having gone forth in the teaching of the Conqueror and failing to find a firm footing therein, he has returned to the low life;
what will this man, who does not practice it himself, awaken to through the teaching of the Conqueror? What fault is there in the teaching of the Conqueror?
Or again, Great King, it is as if a man were gravely ill and [sought] one skilled in the arising of diseases, whose work is unfailing, constant, and successful.
“Suppose a man, having seen a physician and surgeon, were to turn back while still afflicted by disease, refusing to have himself treated.
In that case, whom would people blame: the patient or the physician?
“The patient, venerable sir, people would blame, saying: ‘This physician was skilled in the origin of diseases and possessed of unfailing, constant success in his practice.’”
“Having seen a surgeon and having had him treat [the wound], he returned still afflicted by the disease;
why should the physician himself treat him who was having him treated? What fault is there in the physician?
“In the same way, Great King, the Tathāgata has placed within the casket of his teaching only that which is capable of completely pacifying the entire multitude of diseases of the defilements.”

He administered the ambrosial medicine, thinking: "Whosoever, being conscious and wise, are oppressed by the disease of the defilements, shall, having drunk this ambrosial medicine, bring all the diseases of the defilements to cessation.
If anyone, without drinking that ambrosial medicine, returns with their defilements still present and reverts to the lower life, it is for that very person...
People will criticize him, saying: "Having gone forth in the teaching of the Conqueror and failing to find a firm footing therein, he has returned to the low life.
What is the use of this teaching of the Conqueror awakening itself if it does not awaken such a person? What fault is there in the teaching of the Conqueror?
Or again, Great King, it is like a hungry man who goes to a great distribution of food for the meritorious and [leaves it].
“If someone were to turn back hungry without having eaten their meal, whom would people blame there: the hungry person or the one who provided the merit-food?
“The hungry person, Bhante, people would blame, saying: ‘This man, though oppressed by hunger, received merit-food but turned back hungry without eating it.
How can food enter his own mouth simply by not eating?’”
“What fault is there in the food?

“In the same way, Great King, the Tathāgata placed within the casket of the Dispensation the most excellent, peaceful, auspicious, sublime, deathless, and supremely sweet food of mindfulness directed to the body, [thinking]:
‘Whoever has their inner self scorched by the defilements and whose minds are overwhelmed by craving...’”
"The wise who possess consciousness, having eaten this food, will eliminate all craving for existence in the realms of sense-desire, form, and formlessness.
If anyone, without eating that food, turns back while still bound by craving and returns to the lower life, people will surely censure him, saying:
"This man, having gone forth in the teaching of the Conqueror and failing to find firm footing therein, has returned to the lower life."
"Why do you yourself awaken one who does not practice this teaching of the Conqueror? What fault is there in the teaching of the Conqueror?

"If, O Great King, the Tathāgata were to ordain only a householder who had already been disciplined in a single fruit [of the path], then this going-forth would not be for the sake of abandoning defilements or for purification; there would be no purpose served by the going-forth.
It is just as if, O Great King, a man having had a reservoir dug by many hundreds of laborers were to announce it thus to the assembly:"
‘Sirs, let none of you who are defiled enter this pond; rather, enter this pond only those who have shaken off dust and dirt, who are pure, stainless, and polished.
Now, Great King, would there be any need for that pond for those who have shaken off dust and dirt, who are pure, stainless, and polished?”
“Certainly not, venerable sir. For those for whose sake they would go to that pond, their business would have been accomplished elsewhere; what need would they have for that pond?

“In the same way, great king, if the Tathāgata were to ordain a householder who had already been disciplined in one fruit [of the path], their task would have been accomplished right there; what need would they have for the going forth?

Or again, great king, it is like a physician who eats the food provided by the assembly, who has mastered the words of the heard mantras, who is free from speculative reasoning, and who is skilled in the arising of diseases.”
A physician, a surgeon whose actions are unfailing, constant, and successful, having gathered together medicines for the pacification of all diseases, might announce to the assembly:
"Sirs, let none who are afflicted by disease come into my presence;
let only those who are free from disease and healthy come into my presence."
“Great King, would there be anything further for that physician to do for those who are free from disease, healthy, whole, and elated?

“No indeed, venerable sir. Whatever purpose they might have had for approaching that physician and surgeon would already have been accomplished elsewhere; what need would they have for that physician?

“In the same way, Great King, if the Tathāgata were to ordain a householder who has already been disciplined in one fruit [of the path], the task would have been completed right there; what need would there be for his going forth?”
Or again, Great King, suppose some man were to have various hundredfold preparations of food, including rice-porridge, prepared and announce to his assembly:
"Sirs, let none of you who are hungry approach this distribution hall;
rather, let those who have eaten well, are satisfied, satiated, nourished, refreshed, and full approach this distribution hall."
“Great King, would there be anything further for those who have eaten, are satisfied, well-fed, nourished, gratified, and full to need by means of that food?
“No indeed, Bhante. Whatever purpose they had for going to that distribution of food, that has already been accomplished by them elsewhere; what use would they have for that distribution of food?

“In the same way, Great King, if the Tathāgata were to ordain a householder who has already been disciplined in the first fruit [of the path], then their task would have been accomplished right there; what use would there be for their ordination?”
Moreover, Great King, those who turn back toward the lower life demonstrate five incomparable virtues of the Victor’s teaching. What are the five? They demonstrate its vastness;

they demonstrate its state of utter purity and freedom from stain; they demonstrate that it is not to be associated with by evil persons; they demonstrate its difficulty of penetration; and they demonstrate that it must be protected by many restraints.
How do they demonstrate the greatness of the earth?

Great King, it is just as when a man who is poor, of low birth, without distinction, and lacking in intelligence, having obtained a great kingdom, very soon falls away, is consumed, and declines from his fame; he is unable to maintain his sovereignty.
What is the reason?
Because of the greatness of his sovereignty.
In the same way, Great King, those who— being without distinction, having performed no merit, and being devoid of wisdom— go forth in the teaching of the Conqueror,
being unable to sustain that most excellent and supreme going-forth, will before long fall away from the teaching of the Conqueror.
Having donned [the robes] and having fallen away, they revert to the inferior state; they are unable to uphold the teaching of the Victor.
What is the reason?
Because of the greatness of the ground of the Victor’s teaching.
In this way they show the greatness of the earth.
How do they show its state of being utterly pure and stainless?
Great King, it is just as water, when it falls upon a lotus leaf, scatters away, disperses, and dissolves; it does not remain there, nor does it adhere to it.
What is the reason?
Because the lotus is pure and stainless.
Even so, Great King, those who are crafty, deceitful, crooked, devious, and holders of false views regarding the teaching of the Conqueror—
They go forth, but before long, having scattered, dispersed, and destroyed that pure, stainless, thornless, bright, excellent, and supreme teaching,
they fail to remain steadfast and, being unstained by it, they revert to the lower life.
What is the reason for this?
Because of the utterly pure and stainless nature of the Victor’s dispensation,
they thus demonstrate its state of being pure and stainless.
How do they demonstrate the state of not associating with evil ones?
Just as, Great King, the great ocean does not dwell with a dead corpse; whatever dead corpse there is in the great ocean, it quickly carries to the shore or casts up onto dry land.
For what reason?
Because the great ocean is the abode of great beings.
In the same way, Great King, whatever wicked, unrestrained, shameless, unrighteous, lazy, indolent, defiled,

and evil persons go forth in the teaching of the Conqueror, they will before long depart from the teaching of the Conqueror— which is the abode of the great beings who are Arhats, stainless, and whose taints are exhausted—
and having failed to dwell there, they fall back into the low life.
What is the reason?
Because the teaching of the Conqueror is not to be associated with evil ones.
Thus they demonstrate the state of being unassociated with evil ones.
How do they demonstrate its state of being difficult to penetrate?
Just as, O Great King, those who are unskilled, untrained, lacking in craft, and devoid of intelligence—archers who are unable to pierce the tip of a hair—stumble and retreat.
What is the reason for this?
Because the tip of a hair is so delicate,
subtle, and difficult to penetrate. In the same way, Great King, those people who are of little wisdom, dull, mute, deluded, and slow-witted,
who go forth in the teaching of the Conqueror, being unable to penetrate that penetration of the four truths which is supremely delicate and subtle—
Having slipped away from the Victor’s dispensation and departed, they soon return to the lower life.
What is the reason?
Because the Truths are supremely subtle, delicate, and difficult to penetrate.
Thus they show its state of being difficult to penetrate.
How do they show its state of being protected by many restraints?

Great King, it is just as if some man, having entered a vast field of battle, were surrounded on all sides by the enemy army from every direction; seeing people approaching with swords in their hands, he would, out of fear, shrink back, turn away, and flee.
What is the reason?
Out of fear for protection from the front lines of various kinds of battle.
In the same way, Great King, those who are evil, unrestrained, shameless, unrighteous, impatient, fickle, and wavering—
Fickle are those foolish people who go forth in the Dispensation of the Conqueror;
being unable to guard the manifold rules of training, they shrink back, turn away, and flee, and before long they return to the lower life.
What is the reason for this?
Because the teaching of the Conqueror is to be protected by many kinds of restraints, they thus demonstrate its state of being protected by many kinds of restraints.

"Great King, even in the most excellent *vassikā* grove, there are flowers pierced by insects; those buds, having closed up, fall away prematurely, yet when they have fallen, the *vassikā* grove is not thereby disparaged."
Whatever flowers are situated there, they pervade every direction and sub-direction with their excellent fragrance.
In the same way, Great King, those who have gone forth in the teaching of the Conqueror but then return to the low life are like jasmine flowers that have been crushed in the Conqueror’s teaching;
devoid of beauty and fragrance, their conduct is unsightly, and they are incapable of flourishing.
And by their returning to the lower life, the teaching of the Conqueror is not said to be disparaged.
Those monks who remain therein pervade the world together with its devas with the fragrance of their excellent virtue.
Just as, O Great King, when a species of rice called *karumbhaka* arises among healthy red rice plants and perishes midway, the red rice is not said to be disparaged because of that destruction.
The rice that grows there is for the king’s enjoyment.
In the same way, Great King, those who have gone forth in the Conqueror’s teaching but return to the low life are like the *karumbhaka* seeds among the red rice;
they do not grow or reach full maturity within the Conqueror’s teaching, but return to the low life midway.
And by their returning to the lower state, the teaching of the Conqueror is not said to be disparaged.
Those monks who remain therein are worthy of Arahatship.
Great King, even for a wish-fulfilling gem, a single rough spot may arise; yet because of the arising of that rough spot, the precious gem is not said to be disparaged.
Whatever is pure in that jewel brings joy to people.

In the same way, Great King, those who have gone forth in the teaching of the Conqueror but return to the lower life are like the rough scabs on the teaching of the Conqueror; yet, by their returning to the lower life, the teaching of the Conqueror is not truly disparaged.
Those monks who remain steadfast therein bring joy to gods and humans alike.
Even for red sandalwood, O Great King, which is perfect in its species, a certain portion may become rotten and foul-smelling.
Yet because of that, the red sandalwood is not called "despised.
That which in it is unrotten and fragrant pervades and overpowers everything around it.

"In the same way, Great King, those who, having gone forth in the teaching of the Victor, return to the lower life, are to be discarded from the teaching of the Victor like a putrid portion within a block of red sandalwood heartwood;
yet, by their returning to the lower life, the teaching of the Victor is not thereby disparaged.
Those bhikkhus who remain therein anoint the world together with its devas with the fragrance of the excellent sandalwood of their virtue."

“Excellent, venerable Nāgasena! By various appropriate and corresponding reasons, you have demonstrated that the teaching of the Conqueror is irreproachable and have illuminated its supreme excellence;
even those who have turned back to the inferior way only serve to further illuminate the supreme excellence of the Conqueror’s teaching.
Thus ends the fifth dilemma: On Turning Back to the Inferior Way.
